item.title: Why Do Parasocial Relationships Feel So Good?
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

Why Do Parasocial Relationships Feel So Good?

Media figures fulfill our own need to be seen.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Social media blurs lines, making parasocial bonds more frequent and intense today.
  • Direct eye contact from media figures triggers real feelings of personal connection in viewers.
  • Parasocial relationships can fulfill human needs for recognition and feeling "seen."

A news anchor looks directly into the camera and says, “Here’s what you need to know.” A podcast host speaks in a calm, familiar tone on your morning walk. An influencer films from a bedroom, looking straight ahead, sharing something personal.

After enough exposure, many people begin to feel they know these figures. Not in a literal sense, of course. They know the relationship is one-sided. And yet the feeling can be surprisingly real.

Psychologists have a name for this experience: parasocial interaction. The term was introduced in 1956 by Donald Horton and Richard Wohl to describe the illusion of a face-to-face relationship with a media figure. Their insight was that certain performers do not simply deliver information. They create the feeling of personal connection through direct address, familiarity, and repeated exposure. The audience is not just watching. They are being drawn into something that resembles a social encounter.

The Building of a Parasocial Connection

What makes this psychologically powerful is that the cues involved are often the same ones our minds use in everyday life to register attention and connection. Eye contact is one of the clearest examples. In ordinary social settings, direct gaze is a potent signal. It captures attention, increases self-awareness, and suggests that another mind is oriented toward us. Reviews of gaze research show that direct gaze has robust effects on attention, memory, and social processing, in part because it signals interpersonal relevance.

On screen, direct gaze can produce a similar effect, even though the person is not actually looking at any one viewer. When a journalist, creator, or celebrity looks straight into the camera, part of the social brain responds as if a reciprocal moment has occurred. The viewer knows, at one level, that this is mediated communication. But another part of the mind still registers the cues of being addressed directly.

This helps explain why direct address matters so much. In a 2024 study, viewers reported a more intense parasocial experience when a journalist addressed them directly rather than indirectly. That stronger parasocial feeling, in turn, was associated with higher ratings of journalist credibility, message credibility, and enjoyment. In other words, when the format made the interaction feel more personally directed, viewers felt more connected—and more inclined to trust what they were seeing.

Earlier work points in the same direction. Hartmann and Goldhoorn found that parasocial experience was strengthened when a media performer used bodily and verbal cues that more closely resembled direct social interaction. Subsequent research has similarly treated eye gaze and direct address as especially powerful triggers of parasocial experience. These cues do not create real mutual knowledge, but they can create the feeling of social presence.

article continues after advertisement

Parasocial Interaction and the Human Need for Recognition

This is where the topic becomes especially interesting from the perspective of Being Seen, the topic of my forthcoming book. Human beings do not only want information. They also want recognition. They want to feel noticed, addressed, and held in another person’s awareness. In real relationships, that feeling is built through mutual attention over time. In mediated relationships, some of the same feelings can be evoked by much thinner cues: eye contact, familiarity, disclosure, repetition, and tone.

It doesn’t mean parasocial relationships are fake in the sense of emotionally meaningless. For many people, they can be comforting, motivating, and genuinely companionate. Research has even suggested that parasocial relationships can function as social surrogates under some conditions, helping meet needs for connection when direct social contact is lacking. The emotional response is real, even if the reciprocity is not.

But parasocial closeness can also blur an important distinction: the difference between being looked at and being known.

When someone on a screen looks directly into the camera, the viewer may experience a small but powerful illusion of mutuality. It can feel as though the person is speaking to them, seeing them, understanding them. Yet the actual relationship remains one-sided. The viewer may know a great deal about the media figure’s style, opinions, routines, and emotional cues, while the figure knows nothing specific about the viewer at all.

This matters because the feeling of being seen is psychologically potent. It lowers distance, increases trust, and makes influence more effective. If a person feels familiar, warm, or personally relevant, their words may carry more weight than the same words delivered in a colder, more impersonal format. That is part of what makes parasocial bonds so useful in media, politics, journalism, and advertising.

article continues after advertisement

How Social Media Intensifies Parasocial Experiences

At a broader level, parasocial interaction reveals something important about the human mind. We are highly responsive to the cues of attention and don’t require full reciprocity to begin feeling connected. This may be even more true now than in Horton and Wohl’s era. Social media creators speak directly to followers, respond occasionally in comments, disclose personal details, and cultivate a tone of intimacy. The boundary between public performance and personal address has become thinner. As a result, the feeling of “I know this person” can emerge more easily and more quickly.

Do Parasocial Relationships Serve Psychological Needs?

Parasocial relationships may serve a real psychological function. For people who feel lonely, isolated, or emotionally undernourished, they can offer comfort, familiarity, and a sense of connection. They should not be dismissed as trivial simply because they are one-sided. The feelings they evoke can be meaningful, and in some circumstances they may genuinely help people feel less alone.

At the same time, they are not a substitute for real relationships. However emotionally powerful they may be, parasocial bonds do not involve mutual knowledge, shared responsibility, or the reciprocal recognition that human relationships need. They may soothe loneliness, but can’t fully replace the experience of being known by someone who has an inner life of their own and can respond freely, imperfectly, and authentically.

That’s why some caution is warranted. Parasocial relationships may help fill an emotional gap, but if they begin to replace rather than supplement real-world connection, the relief they provide may come at a cost. Their value is real, but so are their limits. The challenge is not to dismiss these bonds, but to understand what they can offer—and what they can’t.

item.title: When a Narcissist Refuses to Use Your Chosen Name
item.description:
Narcissism

When a Narcissist Refuses to Use Your Chosen Name

How name misuse can be a tool of power and control.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Persistent name misuse is a disguised form of dominance.
  • A person's name is part of their identity, and it's not up for interpretation or debate.
  • Narcissists can react with rage when presented with a boundary.

“Remember that a person’s name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language.”—Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People

What we call ourselves is precious to us and a key part of our identity. It’s how we present ourselves to the world; it’s tied to our history, our sense of self, and our culture. When someone calls us by the wrong name, it’s usually a simple mistake, and an apology is made. However, narcissists will intentionally and consistently call you the wrong name to exert power and control.

How a Narcissist Uses Your Name

How the narcissist changes your name can be subtle or jarring. They will call you by another version of your name, your middle name, or a different name entirely; for example, you go by Rob, and the narcissist insists on calling you Robert or Bobby. A narcissist may also repeatedly call you by an incorrect name, even though you have stated your name clearly. They may intentionally mispronounce your name, claiming your pronunciation "isn't correct.” They may make a derogatory play on words with your name or use alliteration. “Jill” becomes “Jealous Jill” because, when you were 3, you tried to take your cousin’s doll from her (which was developmentally appropriate behavior). Except now, you’re 30, and the narcissist still insists on calling you that.

Control Disguised as Familiarity

When narcissists use an incorrect name, they are exerting power and control. They have a sense of superiority, and there's no more effective method to communicate this than to tell someone, “I know what you should be called better than you do.” Renaming someone is a form of dominance. It also implies familiarity with you that is false. Others may think that the narcissist is close to you because they call you by a “special” name.

When the narcissist gives you a “new” name, they are telling you that their needs and preferences override yours. They are signaling that what they want is most important, even above what someone wants to call themselves. It’s a powerful way to take away someone’s autonomy. If the narcissist is sending the message that they know best what to call you, then it is more likely that they are telling you other ways you should be “better.”

It Keeps You Off-Balance

When a narcissist calls you by another name, it is a constant reminder of their power and control. In addition, it is degrading to be called a name different from the one you specifically requested they use. The underlying message they send is that you aren’t important enough for me to care about your needs. That would require a level of empathy that they may not possess. Intentionally using a different name is a power play. It can cause exhaustion on your part. Do you keep correcting them? Or because they are so reactive to any perceived criticism, do you just answer to the name the narcissist has bestowed on you?

What You Can Do

If you recognize this pattern from one or more people in your life, here are some practical ways to respond.

  • Say your name clearly and only once. You don’t owe anyone repeated explanations for why you want to be called by your own name. State your preference directly. “I go by Jill, not Jillian. Please use that.” You have done your part by being clear and assertive. If you are called the incorrect name, you may consider not responding until they say your name correctly. You are enforcing a boundary.

  • Don’t apologize for wanting your name used correctly. You have the right to be called whatever you choose. The narcissist may tell you that you are “so sensitive,” or “always making a big deal out of nothing.” Remember, this is the narcissist’s issue, not yours.

  • Refuse to engage in an argument. Narcissists don’t respond respectfully when people set boundaries. Take it as a sign that you were right to set the boundary. Walk away from the conversation.

  • Consider going low-contact or no-contact. If this person continually disrespects you by not calling you by your chosen name, chances are they’ve shown you disrespect in other areas of your life. Consider how much contact you truly want with this person. You might want to speak with a mental health professional to consider your options.

You don’t need anyone’s permission to decide what you want to be called. You have a right to your chosen name.

item.title: Heading to College Orientation? Here's What You Should Know
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

Heading to College Orientation? Here's What You Should Know

16 things to consider when attending college orientation.

Posted June 23, 2026

College is a huge investment on many levels, and it’s understandable that parents and students would approach college orientation programs this summer with mixed feelings and trepidation. There’s the excitement for sure, but there’s also the fear and worry. Did my student choose the right college? Will they adjust and make friends easily? What do they really need to be successful? How can I balance being supportive and also letting go?

Source: Meredith Spencer / Unsplash

As a college professor for over 30 years and the author of a new college guide, The Complete U: Over 100 Lessons for Success in and out of the College Classroom, I want to offer you some things you might consider investigating when you attend orientation in advance of starting college in the fall.

1. What sort of activities will be happening during welcome week?

2. What support services are in place, should I need them? This includes things like counseling, tutoring, academic success workshops, library research assistance, and time management workshops.

3. Walk around and explore the campus to find where things are located and to scout out hidden gems you’ll want to return to, such as a nearby arboretum, a great campus café for studying, the library, etc.

4. Ask privately about any accommodations needed for dining.

5. Seek help from an advisor about your class schedule and a good plan for early success.

6. Find out the school's policy on AI.

7. Locate things now before they become a potential crisis. This includes therapy, health services, a dentist, etc. In fact, look for health services and find out their hours.

8. Schedule an appointment with the financial aid office.

9. Ask to see the residence hall where you’ve been assigned to live and get the room dimensions and other features to know about the room so you can plan accordingly.

10. Locate the IT office. They can be a great help if you’re having trouble with email access, the learning management platform your school uses, online classes, and other troubleshooting. Plus, if your computer dies, they can often loan you a laptop for a period of time so your studies are minimally disrupted.

11. See if you can get things early, like your ID and parking pass.

12. Try to connect with a few other new classmates and families. It will be reassuring to see familiar faces when you arrive on campus in the fall.

13. Find out where certain things are located in the area surrounding campus. For example, it’s helpful to know where there’s a pharmacy, a grocery store, a pet store if you’re bringing an animal, a hardware store, a good coffee shop, and a place you enjoy, perhaps a bookstore or movie theater.

14. Find out where the gym and recreation center are located, as well as hours and schedules for things like yoga classes, the pool, the weight room, etc. There are often times that are reserved for student-athletes, and it’s good to know when things are available for you. Plus, once you know your class schedule and have this information, you can start to think about and plan how you will take care of yourself, which supports feeling more confident and in control.

15. Grab schedules for campus events, concerts, and games. Sometimes the paper versions, when available, serve as better visual reminders when posted on a board in your room, on the fridge, etc.

16. Find out about late-night security and escorts to walk you back to your residence hall.

item.title: Avoidance Can Literally Shrink Your World if You Let It
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Avoidance Can Literally Shrink Your World if You Let It

Personal Perspective: A tale of avoidance, jet lag, and recovering one's dreams.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Sometimes one negative experience can turn into prolonged—and unnecessary—avoidance.
  • An abandoned lifelong dream or passion can be worth re-examining.
  • An inner voice may nudge you to turn back toward something you once loved.
Source: Pixabay/JESHOOTS-com

Years ago, I spent a milestone birthday week in Florence and experienced unbearable jet lag.

Smartphones weren’t a thing, and the only available internet connection was a computer in a locked common area. I’d long finished the couple of books I’d brought and spent my nights flipping through indecipherable, depressing Italian television channels.

My mother is European. I grew up traveling to Europe every few years to see her family. I first set foot in Italy on a backpacking trip with my boyfriend in medical school. I was instantly captivated. A dream of living there one day was born, and I soon returned with friends and even a couple of times on my own.

But after the experience in Florence, I wrote off Italy and transatlantic travel in general. It was like a switch got turned off. The dream was gone; that part of my life was over. The experience in Florence had been so disappointing, lonely, and awful that I was not willing to ever risk it again.

In the spring of 2024, I was driving to Spokane airport to catch a flight to Atlanta, where I’d be giving a speech. I listened to a contemplative meditation/reflection app as I drove and reflected on a prompt about what I needed to do most.

The words that came to mind: “Go to Italy.”

My internal reaction was a fierce, resounding “no." I was never going to risk that again; I work too hard to spend another week of vacation in misery.

More words came to mind: “But you used to love Italy.”

Yes, I did. And something about that moment flipped the switch back. On the flight, I booked my ticket and AirBnB.

I then remembered that while attending a lecture on sleep at a Harvard Medical School Continuing Education course, I had heard a leading sleep researcher mention their favorite jet lag app.

When I got back from Georgia, I found my notes from that course, and the name of the app.

I entered my flights into the app and followed the instructions to the letter. It was all based on light exposure and entrainment of circadian rhythms. Sunglasses in the evening pre-trip to block light and start shifting my system. Early morning light exposure upon arriving at my destination. Planned sleep and wake times for the first few days, and more.

I experienced no jet lag. Zero. The first afternoon in Italy I was a little sleepy, but nothing bothersome. I felt great.

Turns out, the reason I hadn’t shifted my circadian clock on that fateful trip to Florence was that it was December. It was cloudy and rainy with little daylight, and because I was on my own, I went to bed when I was tired, even if it was dinnertime. All my prior trips to Italy had been in summer or early fall, so my internal clock was naturally reset by the bright sunlight, outdoor meals, and activity.

article continues after advertisement

After my return to Italy, I rediscovered and reclaimed my passion for that exquisite country. I’ve gone several more times and hope to never stop. It also helped me recover from the recent end of a very difficult marriage.

This week, I’ll return to what is now my home away from home in Southern Italy. My adopted Italian “family” awaits, and I’m intentionally eating less this week because of all the prosciutto, pizza, pasta, bread, and wine I’ll shortly be showered with.

Yes, the anti-jetlag app was transformative.

But more importantly, I want to make sure I never shut down or shrink my life again based on one bad experience. And I hope you don’t either.

item.title: When Does It Matter If a Leader Is Popular?
item.description:
Leadership

When Does It Matter If a Leader Is Popular?

Leaders' longevity depends on perceived trajectory, not current popularity.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Leaders survive based on the systems that grant them power, not their personal popularity.
  • Parliamentary politics in Britain offers low shelter from removal by peers.
  • Football managers are judged by results, which can shield them from the ups and downs of fan opinion.
  • In both politics and football, a leader's longevity depends on perceived trajectory, not current popularity.

On the weekend of June 20-21, 2026, leaders of two British institutions were under great pressure. Sir Keir Starmer, the prime minister, was deciding whether to resign after more than 100 of his own party’s MPs called for his departure. Thomas Tuchel was managing the England men’s football team through the group stage of the FIFA World Cup under the long shadow of a predecessor, who, despite relentless criticism, delivered the team’s best sustained run in 60 years.

Neither leader’s popularity was at its lowest ever. But confidence in neither of them could be described as high.

In late 2025, Ipsos rated Starmer’s popularity at -66, the lowest ever recorded for any British prime minister. By the time Starmer announced his resignation, on June 22, his popularity had improved slightly, to -60. But even this was lower than Liz Truss’s previously record-breaking score of -59 in 2022, at the end of the briefest premiership in British history.

Similarly, in a Betfair/YouGov poll in September 2025, nearly a year after Tuchel’s appointment, only 28 percent of respondents considered him to be the right man for the job. Following England’s 4-2 defeat of Croatia last week, confidence in his leadership appeared to rise, with the percentage of supporters believing England could go on to win the World Cup doubling from 12 percent before the match to 24 percent afterwards.

When Does Popularity Matter?

Such statistics, and their seemingly tenuous connection to leaders’ longevity, raise the question: Does it really matter whether or not a leader is popular?

The instinctive answer, whether in politics, football, or any other field of human endeavor, is: Yes. Leaders need followers. If you lose the room, you lose the ability to lead. But a closer look at the conditions under which different leaders operate reveals a more complicated picture. Some leaders hold on to power for years in the face of sustained public opposition. Others are dispatched quickly to the dustbin of history despite their popularity.

What seems to matter isn't popularity per se. It's the system within which that popularity functions. Some systems convert unpopularity directly and quickly into removal. Others shelter leaders from the impact of public opinion.

British parliamentary politics is a low-shelter system. Members of parliament can remove a prime minister without a general election. There are no fixed terms or institutional buffers to protect the “first among equals” from being fired by their peers. An informal erosion of confidence in his or her capacity to lead is ultimately all it takes to topple the leader.

Football operates differently. Failures cannot be papered over with reports or buried in committees. A manager’s performance is measured by what his or her team does on the pitch. Team selection, training, and tactics matter, but only up to a point. As the late Nottingham Forest manager Brian Clough put it: "We had a good team on paper. Unfortunately, the game was played on grass."

High-Shelter vs. Low-Shelter Systems

The clarity of score-keeping in football is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it exposes managers to the impatience of boards and supporters when results are poor. But on the other hand, it renders a coach’s personal popularity less relevant. As long as the wins keep coming, criticism of a manager’s leadership or frustration with their methods can be dismissed as noise: sound and fury, signifying nothing.

The tenure of Thomas Tuchel’s predecessor, Gareth Southgate, is a case in point. During his eight years as England manager, his popularity seesawed between national treasure and object of derision. He was alternately praised for inspiring the team’s confidence and criticized for a defensive playing style that failed to capitalize on the wealth of attacking talent at his disposal. During Euro 2024, his approval ratings fluctuated wildly, hitting a low of 43 percent shortly before the quarter-finals, only to rebound to a high of 69 percent just before the final.

Tuchel inherited little if any of the warmth people felt towards Southgate. But he did inherit the structural shelter of a system in which the manager serves at the pleasure of the English Football Association rather than the court of public opinion. That’s why he’ll outlast Starmer. As long as the English FA believes he has the capacity to bring the results the nation craves, they’ll continue to back him. In contrast, members of Labor’s enormous parliamentary majority stopped believing in Starmer’s ability to turn things around or win back enough of the nation’s support to get them re-elected.

In leadership, what matters is not the leader’s current popularity but his or her perceived trajectory.

item.title: The Unspoken Reason Cofounders Pull Back
item.description:
Leadership

The Unspoken Reason Cofounders Pull Back

Tension between business partners often involves hidden emotional dynamics.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Performance gaps between cofounders are rarely about laziness; they're often relational.
  • Withdrawal, role erosion, and emotional debt most often drive the gap between cofounders.
  • The friction in cofounder dynamics is almost always mutual, even when it doesn't feel that way.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

A founder I worked with, let's call her Sarah, had built a profitable company with her cofounder for six years.

From the outside, the business looked healthy: $10M revenue, a growing team, a product people respected. Inside, they hadn't spoken live for months. Every interaction was routed through Slack or email, carefully engineered to avoid friction. Sarah had stopped including her cofounder in product decisions. Her cofounder had stopped pushing back.

They both described it as a workflow problem.

It wasn't.

What looked like a work problem had been building for a long time. And it's more common than most founders want to admit.

The Pattern Isn't Laziness

When one cofounder appears to be underperforming, the instinctive read is personal: They've lost motivation, they're not committed, they're coasting. That read is usually wrong, or at the very least, incomplete.

Research on startup teams suggests that 65 percent of high-potential ventures fail due to cofounder conflict, not market fit or funding (Wasserman, 2012). But the conflicts that sink companies rarely announce themselves. They first tend to show up as performance gaps, role drift, and communication that gets progressively more transactional.

Across dozens of cofounding teams, three patterns show up repeatedly:

  1. Withdrawal cycles. When one founder becomes hypervigilant under pressure—taking on more, moving faster—the other tends to do less. Usually, this is an unconscious stress response. The more one founder compensates, the less room the other founder has to contribute. Unfortunately, the psychologist John Gottman identified stonewalling—emotional withdrawal during conflict—as one of the most reliable predictors of relationship breakdown (Gottman & Silver, 1999). Cofounder partnerships aren't immune to these dynamics.
  2. Role erosion. This builds on the withdrawal cycle above. As tension builds, boundaries between roles start to blur. The founder who's "outperforming" begins making decisions in the other's domain out of necessity, frustration, or both. The displaced founder becomes less engaged, often feeling underappreciated for their contributions, which justifies further exclusion. And it compounds.
  3. Emotional debt. Unresolved tension has a way of collecting interest. Conversations become shorter. Assumptions replace curiosity. Small disappointments get filtered through increasingly negative interpretations of the other person's behavior. When founders avoid addressing what's actually wrong between them, accumulated resentment, unspoken hurt, and eroded trust eventually surface as disengagement, criticism, or outright conflict. Over time, each founder becomes more convinced they understand the problem—and less interested in questioning their own perspective.

This unstable foundation doesn't stay contained. Employees notice. They start reading the room instead of doing their work. Important decisions get delayed because the rules are unclear and decision rights feel murkier than ever.

What Sarah and Her Cofounder Found

The structural business complaints—role boundaries, decision rights, who owned what—were real. But they were sitting on top of something more challenging to address.

Sarah's cofounder didn't feel excluded from product decisions as much as she felt cut out of the partnership. Instead of being named directly, the frustration found other exits: critical emails, silence in meetings, and a slow withdrawal that looked, from Sarah's side, like someone checking out. Sarah absorbed more. The gap widened.

What neither of them had done was name any of it directly.

When they finally did, the dynamic shifted. Sarah's cofounder shared that beneath the frustration (and even more importantly), she didn't feel trusted. That landed differently than any performance conversation had. Sarah recognized how her own pattern of suppressing discomfort and carrying everything alone was costing both of them.

The structure was only one part of the problem. The unspoken relational dynamics were the root cause.

3 Things Worth Trying

If you're in a similar dynamic, a few approaches tend to help.

  1. Start with metacommunication, not the business issue. Most of these conversations start too late and in the wrong register, using performance language to describe what is really a relationship problem. A more useful entry point might be: What's getting in the way of us working well on this? It's a small shift, but it shifts the focus back on the relationship dynamics.
  2. Name what's actually happening emotionally. Conversations about output that ignore what's underneath them tend to go nowhere. If you're frustrated, say so. But make sure you don't use accusatory language. "You've been checked out," is less effective than, "I've been feeling isolated in these decisions and I don't think that's working for either of us."
  3. Have the conversation about ownership that you've both been avoiding. Performance drift often starts with ambiguity. Unclear ownership, unspoken expectations about time and commitment, and mismatched assumptions about what this phase of the company often contribute. A direct conversation about who owns what, and what each person needs to do their best work, closes a lot of those gaps.

None of these are instant solutions, but the alternative of compounding drift rarely ends well.

Before You Draw Conclusions

Now is an important moment to notice how much of your experience you are currently holding back from your cofounder. If you notice a buildup, pay attention. Get curious about your contribution to the problem. Ask your cofounder for feedback about how your behavior might be making it harder for them to engage with you.

The friction between cofounders is almost always mutual, even when it doesn't feel that way. The only way to get a more accurate picture of the relationship is to start raising some of these questions and observations.

These dynamics rarely resolve on their own. Left unaddressed, they quietly tax the founders, the team, and eventually the company itself.

item.title: Finding Support Amid Divorce Isolation
item.description:
Divorce

Finding Support Amid Divorce Isolation

How to navigate loneliness and rebuild support systems during divorce.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Support from friends and family fades during divorce, but you can stay connected and emotionally grounded.
  • It's important that newly separated people push themselves to re-engage socially despite discomfort.
  • Therapy can help with separating emotional pain from practical divorce decisions.

One of the most painful surprises of divorce is how isolating it can become.

At the beginning, people are often surrounded by support. Friends call constantly. Family members check in. Everyone wants updates and reassurance that you’re OK. But divorce rarely resolves quickly. And sooner than most people expect, the energy around you changes. Friends who initially leaned in may begin asking, “Is that still going on?” Loved ones who genuinely care may quietly lose patience with the length, complexity, and emotional demands of the process. This mismatch—between how long divorce actually takes and how long supporters tend to remain engaged—is one of the biggest contributors to divorce isolation.

Over time, many people stop talking about what they’re going through, not because they no longer need support but because explaining the realities of divorce becomes exhausting. Particularly in complicated divorces, people often struggle to explain why decisions are being made, why compromises are necessary, or why the process feels so slow. Friends and relatives may unintentionally oversimplify things or may even put the person going through the divorce on the defensive:

  • “Why aren’t you fighting for the house?”
  • “Why would you agree to that?”
  • “My cousin got much more than that in her divorce.”

What people often don’t realize is that the person going through the divorce may be struggling to accept and understand the legal and emotional trade-offs themselves. Having to constantly defend or justify painful decisions can become overwhelming. Sometimes the easiest option feels like silence.

Ask What Kind of Support Is Actually Helpful

One of the biggest mistakes loved ones make during divorce is assuming they already know what support should look like. People often rely on what happened in their own divorce, a sibling’s divorce, or something they read online. But divorce law is deeply individualized, and emotional needs are even more so.

A much more helpful question is simply: “What would be helpful to you right now?”

  • Do they want advice?
  • Do they want someone to listen without trying to fix the problem?
  • Do they want comfort?
  • Do they want distraction?

Many people instinctively rush into fix-it mode when someone they love is struggling. But sometimes a divorcing friend doesn’t want strategy. They don’t want analysis. They don’t want to hear what your cousin’s lawyer did in 1998. Sometimes they simply want someone to sit beside them and let them feel sad without trying to solve it.

And sometimes they do want help: Make a space for your loved one to ask specifically for what they need.

Divorce Is Emotionally Exhausting—And Also Logistically Exhausting

People often underestimate how physically and mentally consuming divorce can be. Yes, there is grief, uncertainty, anger, loneliness, and fear. But there is also paperwork: financial disclosures, insurance changes, utility accounts, retirement beneficiaries, tax records, school logistics, medical coverage, bank statements, parenting schedules. Entire systems of life have to be reorganized.

Even highly competent people can become overwhelmed by the sheer administrative burden of divorce. A person who normally functions beautifully at work may suddenly struggle to complete basic tasks. Loved ones sometimes interpret this as avoidance or irresponsibility. More often, it is overload. Patience, understanding, and offers of administrative help can be very supportive.

Therapy can be particularly important during a litigated divorce. Therapy gives people a structured place to process emotional realities that a judge is not going to deal with. Very few people receive emotional resolution through the legal process. The court system is not designed to heal emotional wounds. It is designed to resolve legal disputes. Understanding that distinction matters enormously so that a person does not prolong litigation, looking for emotional resolution that won’t be found there.

The Legal Process Can Intensify Feelings of Powerlessness

Divorce litigation, in particular, can feel profoundly disorienting. The process is slow and uncertain, and often it does not make intuitive sense to the people living through it. When cases become heavily litigated, people may find themselves in the deeply uncomfortable position of having strangers make major decisions about their finances, homes, and children.

Some people enter a disputed divorce hoping for validation. They want someone to declare them “right.” But divorce court is not structured around winners and losers. Judges are usually trying to reach moderate outcomes. Divorce is not typically an all-or-nothing proposition. It is a series of compromises, trade-offs, and imperfect resolutions.

Emotionally, that can feel devastating. The loss of control is one of the hardest psychological aspects of divorce. People often feel that their future has been placed in the hands of strangers who barely know them. That emotional reality can intensify loneliness and isolation, especially when others around them cannot fully understand the complexity of what they are experiencing.

Don’t Withdraw From Your Life

One of the most important patterns I encourage people to resist is social disappearance. Many newly separated people avoid gatherings because they feel embarrassed attending alone. They worry that people will whisper. They fear awkward questions. They feel exposed without the familiar safety blanket of their marriage.

But in my experience, the anticipation is usually far worse than the reality. The gossip passes very quickly. People move on. And nearly every client I’ve worked with who pushed themselves to re-engage socially—despite discomfort—tells me they are grateful they did. Sometimes I tell clients very directly: “You have to go. Lift your chin up and go.” Because the longer someone surrenders spaces in their life out of shame, fear, or discomfort, the harder it becomes to reclaim them later.

This is particularly important when children are involved. Parents who retreat from school communities, social events, or family activities may unintentionally allow the divorce to consume their identity. Remaining visible in your own life matters.

Be Careful About Taking Advice From Everyone

Support is healthy. Crowdsourced decision-making usually is not. There is a difference between talking through decisions with trusted confidants and taking a poll of everyone you know.

When people seek advice from too many sources, the decision-making process often becomes cluttered with emotional reactions, personal projections, and misinformation. This is especially dangerous during divorce because many people offering advice are unknowingly filtering your situation through their own unresolved experiences. What worked in their divorce may not apply to yours.

The most grounded people during divorce are usually the ones who develop a small, trusted circle rather than constantly seek external validation.

Therapy Helps People Separate Emotion From Decision-Making

One of the most valuable things therapy can do during divorce is help people separate emotional pain from practical choices.

For example, someone may desperately want to keep the marital home because, emotionally, they cannot bear the idea of their spouse getting it. But financially, remaining in the home may not actually be sustainable or might even be financially destructive. Similarly, a parent may feel intense anger toward a co-parent while still needing clarity about what is truly best for their children. Therapy creates space to untangle those things.

Therapy also helps people build emotional regulation during one of the most emotionally challenging periods of their lives. Many divorcing people are living in a near-constant state of emotional activation. Good therapy helps people pause, reflect, and make choices intentionally, rather than simply react out of pain.

And perhaps most important, therapy helps people begin imagining that another chapter exists. Because ultimately, the people who navigate divorce most successfully are usually not the people most focused on what they lost. They are the people who gradually become capable of imagining what might be possible moving forward.

item.title: The Overlooked Impact of Pulling Pet Hair
item.description:
Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors

The Overlooked Impact of Pulling Pet Hair

This trichotillomania-related behavior rarely gets talked about.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Pulling hair off one's pet due to trichotillomania is more common than is typically recognized.
  • Feelings of guilt over pulling a pet's hair can be intense and rooted in the bond with a trusting animal.
  • Compassion, not shame, is central to treating pet-related BFRBs and protecting both the pet and person.

Certain aspects of living with trichotillomania rarely surface, even in spaces specifically created to discuss body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs). This is one of them.

Most individuals living with trichotillomania are well aware of how the condition affects them personally. What comes up far less often in clinical settings, in support groups, and even in the scientific literature is what happens when they are pulling their pet's hair.

It's an uncomfortable topic. For those affected, it often goes unspoken for years. But it is more common than most people recognize, and the individuals living with this behavior deserve a thoughtful, honest conversation rather than silence and shame.

Understanding the Experience

The guilt that accompanies pulling hair from a beloved pet is often intense. It differs from other dimensions of trichotillomania in an important way: It's not simply frustration with oneself for engaging in the behavior, which may have resulted in their own hair loss or skin damage. It's a complex set of emotions around targeting the hair of a pet who loves and trusts them and has no understanding of why this happens. That distinction carries a weight all its own.

Trichotillomania is a psychiatric condition characterized by repetitive hair pulling that is often urge-driven and difficult to stop, despite genuine efforts to do so. Understanding the context in which pulling occurs and the function it serves is central to understanding the condition for a given individual.

For many people, hair pulling serves a self-regulating or self-soothing function, and sensory qualities of the hair itself can play a meaningful role. It follows, then, that a pet's fur, which is often soft, textured, and associated with comfort, can activate and perpetuate the same cycle.

Pulling from an animal in this context is not an expression of cruelty or indifference. It reflects the same underlying mechanism, operating in a different environment. Understanding this is important for the individuals affected and for the clinicians working with them.

What to Look for in Your Pet

Animals cannot communicate discomfort directly, which places the responsibility of observation on their owners. Repeated pulling, even when gentle, can result in:

  • Skin irritation or focal hair loss, particularly in areas pulled from consistently: This can resemble allergic dermatitis or stress-related alopecia, making veterinary evaluation important for accurate assessment and appropriate care.
  • Behavioral changes: Increased avoidance, reactivity, or anxiety around specific people or in particular contexts. Animals are sensitive to both physical discomfort and relational tension, and some will begin to guard or withdraw from environments associated with discomfort or distress.
  • Excessive self-grooming of the site where hair is pulled. This may include persistent licking of the affected area, which can further irritate the skin and lead to secondary skin problems over time.

Any of these signs warrants a conversation with a veterinarian. Uncertain of how to begin the conversation? Describing what you're observing is a sufficient place to begin, and a good clinician will take it from there.

A Path Forward

Effective treatment for BFRBs begins with a thorough functional assessment—understanding the specific contexts, triggers, and functions that maintain the behavior for that individual. That same framework applies here.

Cognitive behavioral therapies with an evidence base for BFRBs share a common foundation: Treatment is individualized, function-informed, and addresses the full range of factors maintaining the behavior. When a pet is part of the clinical picture, a skilled therapist will thoroughly assess what role this pulling context plays as well as other factors that may be relevant, such as whether pulling is automatic, goal-directed, sensory-driven, or self-regulating, amongst many other factors, and intervene accordingly.

Many individuals find that pulling from a pet happens in a particularly automatic, low-awareness state, making awareness training an especially critical starting point for intervention. Stimulus control strategies and environmental modifications can further reduce vulnerability in high-risk situations, without requiring the person to avoid or distance themselves from their pet.

After all, the goal of treatment is not avoidance. Animals provide genuine comfort and joy, and that relationship is worth protecting. The aim is to preserve the connection while interrupting the cycle. With appropriate treatment, that is an achievable goal. And for those in a position to share relevant context with their veterinarian, doing so supports more accurate assessment of any physical effects on the animal and more informed care overall.

Change Begins with Compassion

Individuals who struggle most with hair pulling from a pet are, more often than not, people who very much love their pets. That is not incidental; it is precisely why the experience is so emotionally painful. Shame, however, tends to amplify rather than interrupt the BFRB cycle. It often increases distress, which increases the urge to escape or otherwise do something to cope and self-regulate, which increases vulnerability to the behavior itself.

What creates change is something more difficult: self-awareness, genuine self-compassion, and the willingness to seek appropriate help. Not because the situation has reached some threshold of severity, but because both the person and their pet deserve to thrive.

item.title: The Hidden Control Behind Love Bombing
item.description:
Love Bombing

The Hidden Control Behind Love Bombing

Manipulative language can disguise coercive control as care.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • What feels like profound connection may actually be the start of hidden, destabilizing control.
  • 12-step communities can unintentionally enable narcissistic abuse by misapplying recovery language.
  • High-empathy individuals are especially vulnerable to their attunement being exploited.
Source: Sean Stratton on Unsplash

“The problem is, you can never tell they’re a narcissist when they love bomb you,” Ellie sobbed. “And my sponsor said I had to forgive him and make amends.”

Then she began hyperventilating.

Ellie had been sober for four years and met her husband during her first year of recovery. John was older, charismatic, and sober for 15 years. At meetings, people listened to him with near reverence.

John insisted they should not date because it would be “13th stepping” and violate the rules—yet confessed he had fallen madly in love with her at first sight.

He told Ellie she was special. He claimed he could see deep into her radiant soul. But he also saw how she was getting in her own way and promised to help her fight her demons. She simply needed to trust him, follow his guidance, and work with the sponsor he chose for her.

Underlying Risks in Support and Recovery Systems

Ellie faced two hidden dangers. The first was John’s undiagnosed grandiose narcissism. The second was being embedded in a system of support and influence that did not understand the dangerous complexities of narcissistic abuse.

Many 12-step circles unintentionally reinforce the myth that no one can make you feel anything and that healing depends on releasing resentment, praying for the other person, and making amends.

Love bombing becomes especially dangerous when manipulative partners weaponize therapeutic, spiritual, or recovery language to normalize control and override a survivor’s reality.

The challenge Ellie faced was not simply that John appeared charming and spiritually mature. It was that manipulative language often sounds loving, wise, or even healing in the beginning.

How Love Bombing Functions as a Form of Control

Research increasingly supports what many survivors have struggled to articulate. The first large study establishing that narcissistic abuse can create post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms in romantic partners was published in 2023 (Arabi). Among 1,255 participants, 97 percent reported emotional abuse, 95.1 percent reported gaslighting, 93.2 percent reported stonewalling, 76.2 percent reported induced jealousy, and 78.6 percent reported love bombing.

article continues after advertisement

In my new book, Ten Keys to Staying Empowered in a Power Struggle, I describe control as a defining feature of narcissistic dynamics. Even during the love-bombing phase, control—not love—is often the hidden aim. The goal is to secure attachment, gain influence, and gradually destabilize a person’s trust in their own perceptions.

People with high empathy, vulnerability, or over-giving patterns are often especially at risk because their emotional attunement can be exploited.

Recent research by Setyaningsih and Rakhmawati (2025) examined the hidden meanings embedded in manipulative love-bombing language. One striking finding was that exaggerated affection often shifts quickly into persuasion, then control, and eventually dominance.

This helps explain why early red flags are so easy to miss.

Warning Signs Associated With Love Bombing

Be cautious when intense affection is paired with these warning signs:

  • Excessive certainty too early (“I knew you were the one immediately.”)
  • Flattery mixed with authority (“I see your greatness—and I know exactly what’s wrong with you.”)
  • Accelerated trust or intimacy (Pressuring you to bond, commit, or disclose quickly.)
  • Help that becomes control (“Trust me. Just do what I say.”)
  • Spiritual, therapeutic, or recovery language (Using it to silence healthy anger or boundaries.)

This final point matters deeply.

While many people benefit from 12-step recovery communities, problems arise when ideas like forgiveness, surrender, or making amends are rigidly applied without understanding coercive control or narcissistic abuse.

Sometimes the most dangerous manipulation does not arrive as cruelty. It arrives sounding enlightened, caring, spiritual, or wise.

Ellie’s deepest confusion was not that John seemed cruel in the beginning. It was that he seemed safe.

That may be the most painful truth about love bombing: What feels like profound recognition may actually be the first stage of control.

item.title: 'AI Anxiety' Is a New Workplace Reality
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

'AI Anxiety' Is a New Workplace Reality

Understandable concerns about job loss are part of today's working landscape.

Posted June 23, 2026

An Australian doctor recently noted that a patient said to him, "I think I've got anxiety about AI."

These days, that feeling is all too common. As the doctor, Grant Blashki, an associate professor at the University of Melbourne, discussed in a university publication, the individual wasn't experiencing a panic attack or clinical anxiety. Rather, it was more like a "persistent sense of unease."

Fears about AI replacing human jobs are real and probably all too common.
Source: Cottonbro Studio / Pexels

It was more a feeling "that the world is changing very quickly, that the systems we live within are being redesigned around us and that most of us don't feel particularly consulted or prepared."

This was a nice, concise summary of what I believe an awful lot of employees across the globe are experiencing. And it isn't surprising; a substantive loss of control at work can easily be an anxiety-producing situation.

Understandable Fears

Uncertainty, whether it comes in the form of a new CEO, a reorganization, or a game-changing technology like artificial intelligence, is naturally disturbing to employees. Why wouldn't it be? In the blink of an eye, one's livelihood can be affected.

While a number of aspects of AI are unsettling—its potential for deepfake scams, unwanted surveillance and personal privacy infringements, etc.—the overarching concern affecting workers today involves job loss.

It involves the understandable fear that AI may be able to do many jobs better than humans. Or, if not always better, then at least satisfactorily and often more cost-effectively.

Let's take a quick look at what kind of jobs appear to be more vulnerable to AI takeover, and which jobs aren't.

Job Applicability

At this point, the consensus is that jobs involving functions, for example, like writing, some computer coding, and routine levels of customer service, may well be susceptible to being handled by AI.

At the other end of the spectrum, jobs involving a high level of hands-on, not-easily-substituted human activity seem less susceptible to AI replacement. To use a few heavy-handed examples, it's difficult to imagine AI replacing a plumber fixing a clogged toilet, a roofer replacing leaky shingles, or a surgeon repairing a hernia.

However, given generative AI's ability to grab and digest vast amounts of copy and "learn" to write, it's not at all difficult to imagine AI doing technical writing, preparing marketing materials, how-to brochures, and so on.

To put a bit more meat on these occupational bones, last year Microsoft did a broad analysis of specifically what jobs appeared to be most and least threatened by AI—jobs with high and low "AI applicability" scores. They came up with 40 jobs of each type; below are their top 10 in each category.

High AI applicability

  • Interpreters and translators
  • Historians
  • Passenger attendants
  • Sales representatives of services
  • Writers and authors
  • Customer service representatives
  • CNC (computer numerical control) tool programmers
  • Telephone operators
  • Ticket agents and travel clerks
  • Broadcast announcers and radio DJs

Low AI applicability

  • Phlebotomists
  • Nursing assistants
  • Hazardous materials removal workers
  • Helpers of painters, plasterers, and stucco masons
  • Embalmers
  • Plant and system operators
  • Oral and maxillofacial surgeons
  • Automotive glass installers and repairers
  • Ship engineers
  • Tire repairers and changers

Clouds on the Horizon

Whether or not this Microsoft list proves accurate (and I definitely wouldn't take anything on it as immutable truth), one does see clear patterns emerging. Of course, individual companies and managements do have considerable latitude in how they choose to implement AI. Or not.

But there's no doubt for employees that AI has become a storm cloud on the horizon, and it's becoming part of the working landscape, one that workers and managers will both have to learn to navigate.

item.title: Huntington's Disease and Schrödinger's Cat
item.description:
Genetics

Huntington's Disease and Schrödinger's Cat

Personal Perspective: Quantum mechanics helps illustrate my two potential futures.

Posted June 23, 2026

“Don’t spend a lot of time imagining the worst-case scenario. It rarely goes down as you imagine it will, and if by some fluke it does, you will have lived it twice.” —Michael J. Fox

A Rainy Day

I suspect it’s not the easiest job in the world to tell someone they’re going to die.

It was a rainy day in March when I sat in a room with a neurologist tasked with doing just that. I’d been waiting for weeks to receive the results of the genetic testing I’d undergone, so he didn’t hesitate or keep me in suspense. He just walked in the room, sat down, and came out with it: “You are gene-positive for Huntington’s Disease.”

That was a little over four years ago. Since then, I’ve met with the same neurologist every six months. I go because of one very small, microscopic problem: One of the genes on my chromosomes has a mutation.

One of the perks of going to Northwestern University every six months for checkups: Stan's Donuts :)
Source: Pamela Mallette

Specifically, my huntingtin gene (HTT, which is located on chromosome 4 and is responsible for healthy brain development and nerve cell survival) has an abnormal repeat of a particular combination of nucleotides called a CAG repeat. Anyone with 40 or more repeats will manifest Huntington’s Disease (HD) in their lifetime; it’s just a matter of when. My number? 41.

Tom Petty Said It Best: The Waiting Is the Hardest Part

The disease is not officially diagnosed until people begin exhibiting the most characteristic symptom of HD: involuntary movements known as chorea. According to my doctors, I am still in what is referred to as the prodromal phase of HD (also known as the pre-motor, pre-clinical, or pre-manifest phase). It means that my genetics are set to self-destruct, but the countdown hasn’t yet begun.

People in this phase often experience non-motor HD symptoms (like depression and mood issues, trouble with organization and memory, and subtle changes in coordination) in the years leading up to clinical diagnosis. But the hardest part, at least for me, is the weight of knowing that the worst is coming, without knowing when, or exactly how bad it will be when it does.

Usually, the “when” is mid-life: motor symptoms typically begin in a person’s 30s and 40s. But sometimes, despite the averages, symptoms don’t appear until a person’s 60s or 70s, meaning that some people get to live pretty full lives before the deterioration begins. At 43 years old, I could begin to experience motor symptoms next week, or a decade or more from now.

There’s also a huge degree of variation in symptom severity. Though HD always follows a similar course that ends in death, sometimes the road leading up to it includes more years of mild symptoms than severe ones. The progression is unique to each individual, and there is no way to know exactly what it will look like.

Enter Schrödinger's Cat

My brain often works in pictures, analogies, and metaphors, and when I try to describe what sitting in this tension feels like, my brain (apparently) goes to quantum mechanics.

Source: Geralt / Pixabay

In the famous thought experiment, theoretical physicist Erwin Schrödinger proposed the following: suppose you have a box, and in the box is a cat (because if there’s anything cats love, it’s being confined against their will). Along with the cat is a radioactive substance, a Geiger counter, and a flask of poison. There is a 50/50 chance that atoms in the radioactive material will decay. If any do, the Geiger counter would detect the emitted radiation and trigger a hammer that breaks the flask, releasing the poison and killing the cat (sorry, kitty). In quantum mechanics terms (which talks in maths), the cat, whose state is undetermined until the box is opened, is presumed to be both alive and dead at the same time.

That’s silly, you say. How can a cat be both dead and alive at the same time? Well, it can’t be, and that’s what Schrödinger was trying to point out. But the complexity remains: Until an observer opens the box and can know the cat’s fate, how can one measure, or describe mathematically, the state of the cat?

I don’t know; I’m not a quantum physicist. But I do know I empathize with the cat.

I Am the Cat

What I mean is that being in the prodromal phase is a bit like waiting for the flask to break. The cat represents my future self, and I am trapped inside a box with my poisonous DNA. My odds are worse than the cat’s, because it is with nearly 100 percent certainty that the flask will break: My CAG repeat makes sure of that.

But when it breaks is still anyone’s guess. Maybe, if I’m lucky, it’ll hold off so I get to live as many of my nine lives as possible. Or maybe I’ll somehow end up with a weaker dose of the poison, and it’s not that bad even once it takes effect. Or maybe someone comes up with an antidote between now and then, or even better, a cure: Maybe someone will open the box and let me out.

In other words, when I think of my future, I have two timelines: one in which I am alive and get to see the world, retire, meet my grandchildren, and grow old with a partner, and one in which I am dead in my 50s, like my mother, her mother, and her grandfather, who passed on their genetics to me. Without being able to peer into the box, my future is unknown, and I am both dead and alive.

My cat—(she's a real) Princess Peach Mallette, who is very much alive.
Source: Pamela Mallette

I Am Not the Cat

I recognize that I am not a cat, and that future me is merely a thought experiment. And while I can imagine her facing any number of possibilities, her death narrative has not yet played out. In that sense, I’d like to leave room for some version of a hopeful future. It helps to guard against the despair this disease brings.

I also try to remember that we all pass through death, and none of us knows the hour or the manner. I happen to have one particular version of a potential future that has been presented to me, so I can choose to live in that darkness now, or I can remain in the present, where there is still plenty of light.

I choose the latter. Like a happy kitty, I will bask in the sun as long as possible.

item.title: Your Body Often Knows What's Happening Before You Do
item.description:
Self-Help

Your Body Often Knows What's Happening Before You Do

Listening to early physical cues can improve how you care for yourself.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Many people miss their body's cues because they were taught to push them down.
  • Body signals are invitations to pause and not a warning that something is wrong.
  • Responding to body cues with small grounding practices can prevent overwhelm.
  • Your reactions matter; listen to your body.
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko/ Pexels

There is a moment that most people do not realize is happening, and that is the moment right before you get overwhelmed. Before the tears, the shutdown, or the irritation comes out of nowhere. It is the moment your body tries to get your attention in a subtle and quiet way. A lot of us miss that moment. We do not miss it because we are careless, but because we were taught to push through or to be fine. But the body does not play along with that way forever. It speaks early and honestly, and when we start to notice those early cues, then things begin to make more sense to our minds.

The Body Notices Things First

Your nervous system is always scanning for safety. It is not something that you consciously notice or do, but it is just happening in the background, like breathing or blinking. It also reacts fast. Faster than your thoughts, faster than your explanations, and faster than the stories you tell yourself about being " too sensitive."

You've probably felt these before:

  • You are talking to someone, and suddenly your chest tightens for no obvious reason.
  • You walk into a room, and your stomach drops even though nothing is "wrong."
  • You get home and feel exhausted in a way sleep does not fix.
  • Someone asks how you are doing, and you genuinely do not know.

These are not random. They are signals that our body is telling us something has shifted.

Why We Don't Catch the Signals

Most people were not raised to pay attention to their internal world. Many of us grew up in environments where:

  • Emotions were minimized
  • Calm was expected and not always supported
  • Anger or sadness had consequences
  • Independence was praised above connection
  • Strength meant "don't feel anything"
article continues after advertisement

So we learned to disconnect from our bodies to stay connected to the people around us. That may work for a while... until it doesn't. The body will start speaking louder through anxiety, irritability, shutdown, or that vague sense that something is off.

Your Body Isn't Overreacting

One of the most healing shifts I see in therapy is when someone realizes their body is not being dramatic, but instead it is being honest. Even the reactions you do not like, the urge to withdraw, or the overthinking are attempts at protection. They are old strategies that once helped you survive something hard.

The shift comes when the questions move from "what is wrong with me?" to "what is my body trying to tell me right now?" That shift is life-changing.

The Early Cues

Everyone's cues are different, but here are some common ones:

  • A small tightness in the chest
  • A sudden drop in energy
  • Feeling spacey or disconnected
  • Jaw tension
  • Trouble focusing
  • A sense of urgency that does not match the moment
  • Feeling "off" without a clear reason

These are the whispers that show up long before the meltdown or shutdown.

What You Can Do With Those Cues

Once you start to notice the cues, you can respond earlier. Not with a big intervention, but just with small grounding shifts, such as:

Source: Darina Belonogova/ Pexels
  • Pause for a few seconds
  • Put a hand on your chest or stomach
  • Name what you are feeling physically without jumping into a story
  • Slow your exhale
  • Step away for a moment if you need to

These are not meant to fix anything; instead, they are meant to help you take a second to get back to baseline.

Relearning How to Listen

Healing is not about becoming perfectly regulated. It can be about becoming familiar with your own signals. It is about catching the whisper before it becomes a shout. It is about trusting your body enough to let it guide you instead of treating it like something you have to manage.

Your reactions make sense. Your body is trying to protect you. You do not have to wait until you are overwhelmed to take care of yourself. You can start at the first cue, even if it is quiet.

item.title: When a Patient Can't See Their Own Illness
item.description:
Psychiatry

When a Patient Can't See Their Own Illness

A diagnosis may not change anything if the family is left out of the room.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • HIPAA protects patients, but has no mechanism for illnesses that prevent self-recognition.
  • Families often have crucial insight into a patient’s condition, but the system rarely listens to them.
  • Patient autonomy and protection should be balanced, especially when patients can’t see their illness.
Source: Cory Mogk/Unsplash

Before the manic psychosis I described in earlier posts, I lived a long stretch of polypharmacy and misdiagnosis. It began with a suicidal collapse in 2016, an overdose that left me in a coma for six days. What followed were years of antidepressants and other medications prescribed for what clinicians called major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.

The diagnoses were wrong. The depression was real, but it was the depressive pole of a bipolar illness no one had yet recognized, and the antidepressants prescribed to treat it were the very class of drugs known to destabilize a bipolar brain. Each prescription, written in good faith for the symptom in front of the clinician, quietly poured fuel on a fire none of them could see.

The correct name finally arrived in March 2020, as the world emptied itself for the pandemic. I was involuntarily committed to St. Mary's Hospital in Madison. The behavior I had been experiencing as righteousness had crossed the line into something the law was finally willing to name. A psychiatrist I had never met before—impatient, rushed, with the bearing of a man already late for his next room—diagnosed me for the first time correctly with bipolar I disorder.

What he did not do was nearly everything else. He did not mention anosognosia, the condition that would determine whether I could absorb the diagnosis he had just delivered. He did not ask whether a family member could be brought into the conversation, something the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) permits with patient consent and that good psychiatric practice would have recommended. He did not schedule a family meeting to help the people closest to me understand what bipolar I disorder is, how it presents, what the medications do, what relapse looks like. Instead, he wrote prescriptions and discharged me. It was the same thing that had been done to me, in various forms, for the previous eight years: pills thrown at a problem no one had taken the time to see whole.

It was the diagnosis I had needed for years.

But it was spoken to the wrong person, in the wrong way, in a room emptied of everyone who could have helped me hear it.

As I described last week, I was in the grip of anosognosia: the neurological condition in which a person cannot recognize the very illness destroying them. The diagnosis was being delivered to a self that lacked the ability to hear it. The diagnosis I might have absorbed, even reluctantly, would have arrived through my mother, Linda, a bioethicist and nurse who had watched the pattern build for years. She could have held the weight of those two words, bipolar I, steady enough for me to look at them. She was 20 minutes away in Madison, waiting for a call that did not come.

article continues after advertisement

I was discharged. I went to my father's apartment. The pills sat in my palm. I flushed them, certain I was reclaiming something that had never actually been mine to lose.

That moment, when the right diagnosis met an empty room, is where this story begins.

What the System Can't Read About Some Psychiatric Patients

HIPAA is a good law that does important work, and I have benefited from its protections, as have millions of others. I am not arguing against it in principle.

What HIPAA cannot see, however, is the difference between two things that severe psychiatric illness can pull apart: epistemic authority, the capacity to know what is happening in your own mind, and moral authority, the right to make decisions about your own life. In ordinary cases, these travel together, and the law treats them as one thing. In severe anosognosia, they come apart. The patient still has moral authority, but they have lost the ground on which it would have rested.

The practical consequence is brutal: The worse the illness, the harder it becomes for families to participate in care. Throughout my years of untreated bipolar disorder, I was asked by clinicians whether I wanted treatment, whether I consented to medication, whether I understood my diagnosis. My answers, fluent and confident, were treated as autonomous choice. They were not. They were the illness speaking, in my voice, using my academic training to defend itself.

article continues after advertisement

The system could only read the self I was presenting. It had no mechanism for hearing the self my mother, my brothers, and the friends who had known me longest could see clearly from the outside.

The journalist Daniel Bergner, in The Mind and the Moon—his investigation of contemporary psychiatry and his own brother's experience with bipolar disorder—locates the problem one layer deeper. Psychiatry, Bergner writes, "cannot fully hear individuality so long as the profession clings to scientific authority." To listen, "it would have to embrace the idea of working with patients, of proceeding on footing that is more equal than not." The field's posture of expertise is precisely what blocks the kind of attention that severe psychiatric illness requires.

If psychiatry cannot hear the individual patient, it is doubly unable to hear the people who know that patient best. The psychiatrist and anthropologist Arthur Kleinman, in The Soul of Care, his memoir of caring for his wife through her long decline with Alzheimer's, names what this kind of medicine has lost. "Care becomes a transaction, rather than a relationship," he writes. The profession, he goes on, "routinely disregards" the partners who carry the actual work of caregiving: nurses, allied health professionals, and "especially families." The clinical knowledge those families hold—who the patient was before the illness, what works and what does not—is treated as personal feeling rather than as evidence.

It is evidence. It is, often, the best evidence in the room.

Implications When Someone Can't Recognize Their Illness

There is a deeper question buried in this: Should patients who cannot recognize their illness sometimes be treated against their will?

I do not ask this lightly. As a gay man, I know the history of psychiatric coercion. For most of the 20th century, homosexuality was classified as mental illness, and the machinery of involuntary commitment was turned, with appalling efficiency, against people whose only pathology was who they loved. The antipsychiatry movement that responded was right to be alarmed, and the pendulum needed to swing toward patient autonomy.

But it has swung so far that we have built a system structurally incapable of protecting patients from the harm caused by their own anosognosia: one that honors the illness's preferences as if they were the patient's, and thanks the family for their concern on the way out.

My answer, arrived at after considerable personal cost, is yes, sometimes. Not the broad commitment powers of the asylum era. Something more careful, more humble, more accountable. Psychiatric advance directives, which let people speak for themselves when well to guide care when they are not. HIPAA's existing "listen-only" provisions, used widely, which already permit clinicians to receive information from family without disclosing back. Assisted outpatient treatment statutes, such as Kendra's Law in New York and Laura's Law in California, administered with the rigor the stakes demand. Trained surrogate decision-makers when families and patients cannot reach agreement.

article continues after advertisement

These ideas are not new. The bioethics literature has been working on them for years. The problem is that almost no one outside NAMI advocacy circles has heard of them. Families in crisis are left frustrated and confused, unaware that legal tools exist that might let them participate in care. The first reform we owe families is knowledge of the reforms that already exist.

Source: Wutthichai Charoenburi/Pexels

Imagine the alternative version of my own 2020. The psychiatrist at St. Mary's delivers the bipolar I diagnosis and, before discharge, asks whether a family member can be brought into the conversation. My mother arrives. She does not contradict the diagnosis. She does what her professional training would have allowed her to do: She helps me understand that the illness lives in my brain rather than in the people I had cast as my enemies. She names what she had been watching for years. She holds the weight of those two words long enough for me to look at them.

I cannot know whether that conversation would have lifted the anosognosia. But it might have. Instead, the next five years happened: the substance use, the felony charges, the months in jail, the state forensic hospital. A room she belonged in. A door the law kept closed.

Not every family member is a bioethicist. But every family member who has watched someone they love disappear into severe mental illness carries knowledge the system needs and does not yet know how to use. What we owe them is more than thanks. We owe them the room.
